en: The Scripture on the Disciple Who Died and Was Reborn, translated by the Song dynasty layman Juqu Jingsheng.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove in Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park together with twelve hundred [monks].
He was accompanied by fifty bhikṣus, twelve thousand bodhisattvas, and five hundred disciples endowed with supernormal powers.

At that time, there was a wise lay disciple (*upāsaka*) who had originally followed ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths. Disgusted by the suffering of ritual sacrifices, he renounced them and entered the Dharma. He upheld the precepts without transgression, was diligent and single-minded, applied himself to the recitation of scriptures, delighted in giving, exercised self-restraint and patience, and constantly maintained a heart of loving-kindness. Suddenly afflicted by illness, he subsequently passed away.
When he was on the verge of death, he instructed his relatives and his parents, saying:
"If my illness should lead to my passing, do not enshroud me for seven days."
"If you keep me in mind, do not go against my word.
Thereupon, he suddenly passed away as if dead.
His parents, relatives, and various families acted according to his instructions and kept the corpse for seven days. On the eighth day, the relatives and various families said:
"The deceased has already been in the grave for eight days; he lies there sleeping, knowing nothing at all. You must hurry to prepare the coffin and perform the enshrouding.
His parents said, "Although many days have passed, his body has neither swelled nor become foul-smelling. Let us keep him for a little longer, until the tenth day."
Before his words had even finished, the dead man immediately opened his eyes.
The parents and all the family members, both great and small, leaped for joy; yet, being unable to move him, they all remained together to guard him.
By the tenth day, he was already able to sit up and speak well.
When the people asked him where he had come from and what he had seen, [he replied: "I saw..."
He said:
"Official soldiers came and took me away to a great city. Within it was a large prison;
the prison was pitch black, its four sides were entirely walled with iron, and the city gates were all made of glowing red-hot iron."
The bodies of those bound within the prison are all seated amidst a great fire; from above and below they are scorched and roasted, and blue smoke issues forth.
Some people there cut their flesh with knives and devour it.
Within the prison, there was a king who questioned me, saying:
"What kind of person are you?
For what offense and on account of what have you come to this place?"

Among these, it treats those who commit the five heinous crimes, those who are unfilial toward their parents, and those who are disloyal and untrustworthy toward their sovereign; it treats the dwellings of all such evil persons—how could their offenses possibly be as grave as this?

He replied: "Since my youth, I have been deluded by evil people and served non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika). For a time, out of worldly ignorance, I killed living beings to sacrifice to Heaven and Earth and drank wine;
furthermore, I sought profit in the marketplace, seeking to enrich myself by cheating with measures, weights, and dimensions."

After the assembly, I met with virtuous teachers who instructed me in doing good and led me into the Buddha-way. There, I encountered śramaṇas and practitioners who conferred the five precepts upon me, and I have since practiced the ten wholesome deeds.
"From that time until today, I have not committed evil again; this grace is due to the Enlightened King’s compassion for my inadequacy.
I then bowed my head.
The King immediately rose, joined his palms, and said to me:
"Stop, stop! A person of pure faith should not act in this way!
He then offered me a seat, and I sat down.
The King then summoned his officials and questioned them:
"This person is an unsurpassed, truly authentic disciple; you all shall attain deliverance through him, and you shall only die when his own lifespan has naturally come to an end!"
The spirit and consciousness follow of their own accord as one proceeds to receive rebirth; if one is to be born among the devas, the celestial deities shall come in person to welcome them;
if one is to be born among humans, those from among humans shall come in person to welcome them.
"How can you bring such a venerable person into this place of the five heinous crimes?
The official replied to the king:

"In this world there are many such people who do not fear the laws of the state, who do not fear the four seasons, and whom the five elements do not constrain; neither ghosts, spirits, heaven, nor earth can take them into account. How can you not question even one or two of them?"
Such people roam across the world with reckless disregard, free from all restraint.

There are Dharma masters whom they call śramaṇas—those who have shaved their heads and wear coarse, shabby robes, yet pride themselves on the Dharma and lead many disciples. They move about in the east, west, south, and north without any sense of propriety; they relocate houses, perform burials, marry off daughters, and take wives, showing no regard for the four seasons. They destroy and alter things without deference to royal ordinances or auspicious signs; such as these ought to be disciplined.
The King said: "Stop, stop! Do you truly not understand this Dharma?

One who wears the robes of the Dharma is not to be esteemed or revered by others, nor is he one whom they fear or find difficult to approach; yet he is honored and served by Śakra, Brahmā, and the Moon and Sun—the kings among them—down to emperors, ministers, and commoners alike."

Honoring such a person brings immeasurable merit and enables others to attain the Way; one must not treat such a person with contempt, for those who treat them with contempt seek only suffering and affliction for themselves.
"Quickly consult the registers of names: has his lifespan come to an end or not?
The official addressed the king, saying, "According to the principles of the life-register, he is not yet due to die!"
He still has twenty years remaining of his allotted lifespan.

Because he previously committed evil during his youth and only later desired to perform good deeds, he takes [the merit] from him to cause his associates to slightly diminish their own [negative] influence.
The King asked: "If a person living in this world commits few evil deeds throughout a hundred years, what should be the punishment for such a person's transgressions?
The official replied:

"This person can only live and cannot die; were he to die, he would continue on in succession, destined to undergo the suffering of retribution for thousands and tens of thousands of kalpas, without ever attaining liberation."
Then the king said:
"The disciples of that Buddha possess the precepts and are diligent and tireless, held in high esteem and respect by the heavenly deities.

This is because the Buddha, with a mind protected and directed by great kindness and great compassion, regards the ten directions of the world with these four immeasurable minds. All people, all things, and even the smallest crawling and flying insects—the Buddha feels pity for them all; his merit flows forth throughout the ten directions of the world."
Therefore, Son of the Buddha, since devas, terrestrial spirits, ghosts, and dragons all revere and honor you, how could you be constrained by royal signs, the four seasons, or the five elements?

The grace of the Buddha is like the four oceans and cannot be measured; even the grains of sand along the banks of ten billion Ganges Rivers might still be weighed and their number calculated, yet the grace of the Buddha cannot be measured!
The official addressed the king, saying:
"Does Your Majesty uphold the pure precepts of the Buddha?
The king replied:
"Because I failed to honor the Buddha while he was seated, my transgressions have followed me to make me the King of this Hell.

You who see those within this prison—whether their lifespans have now ended and they do not yet receive [rebirth], or those who dare not come before you—you must all join your palms and rise to go forth and welcome them. Let them be judged according to the wholesome merits they have performed; the deities of merit will naturally come to receive them.
As for those whose deaths are not yet due, they shall have their own protection and quickly attain recovery."

If there are those who have already entered the True Dharma but later regret it and return to being non-Buddhists, sacrificing living beings in worship, then the evil spirits of heterodox paths will find an opportunity upon seeing such views; these individuals thus lack protection for themselves.
Even if one possesses a lifespan of a thousand years, one will inevitably encounter the nine untimely deaths and die of illness despite being free from disease.
The reason for this is that the protective deities do not grant them their aid; such individuals shall ultimately never attain liberation.
"If bhikṣus who uphold the precepts and their disciples should diligently practice six matters. What are these six?
First is the pāramitā of dāna; they should be skilled in giving and must not be stingy."
Second is the *śīlapāramitā*: one should guard and be cautious with moral precepts, never transgressing them;
third is the *kṣāntipāramitā*: one should practice forbearance and restrain the mind, ensuring that neither heart nor speech harbor anger;
fourth is the *vīryapāramitā*: one should exert diligent effort and be energetic, never being indolent.
Fifth is the dhyāna-pāramitā: one should concentrate the mind in single-minded absorption and not be negligent.
Sixth is the prajñā-pāramitā: one should diligently practice the sūtras through oral recitation and become proficient in upāya-kauśalya (skillful means).
These are the six matters that constitute the foundation for a bodhisattva seeking the Way.

Furthermore, there are another six matters—first, the eye; second, the ear; third, the nose; fourth, the mouth; fifth, the body; and sixth, the mind. If a person wishes to seek the Way and receive its blessings, they should guard these six matters.

Guard the eyes and do not cling to forms; guard the ears and do not cling to sounds; guard the nose and do not cling to fragrances; guard the mouth and do not cling to flavors; guard the body and do not cling to tactile sensations; guard the mind and do not cling to sensual desires.
These are the six matters to be protected.
"Furthermore, one should extinguish three matters. What are these three?"
First is lust, second is anger, and third is delusion.
These are the three poisons.
"Furthermore, one should extinguish five things."
What are the five? First, sensation; second, perception; third, volitional formations; fourth, consciousness; and fifth, craving.
These are the five aggregates (skandhas).
"Furthermore, there are the six bases of decay (āyatana).
What are the six bases of decay?

First, the eye is the decay of forms; second, the ear is the decay of sounds; third, the nose is the decay of fragrances; fourth, the mouth is the decay of flavors; fifth, the body is the decay of tactile sensations; sixth, the mind is the decay of mental phenomena.
These are the six decays (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

"The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*), and the three poisons (*triviṣa*) together constitute twenty matters within the body that are constantly present in the human person; when a person practices the Way, they must always sever these twenty matters."
If one cannot prohibit these twenty matters, one shall fall into the offenses of human attachment:
if the six sense-faculties are not severed, one shall fall into the eighteen hells;
if the five aggregates are not severed, one shall transmigrate through the five realms of existence.
"If the three poisons are not severed, one shall enter the three evil realms.

'If a good man or good woman restrains and maintains twenty matters within their body through the precepts—becoming as pure and free from defilement as a mirror cleansed of grime, with inner and outer illumination—is there even one person among the hundreds of thousands of millions of people in the world who is a disciple of the Buddha?'"
The official said,
"In truth, I have none. The king said:
"Judging from this, one knows that the Buddha’s merit is vast and towering, profound and majestic, like the great ocean that cannot be resisted!
The official addressed the king, saying:
"It is truly as Your Majesty has said; it was due to my own fault that I failed to distinguish between the true and the false. I beg to be permitted to send him back."
The King said, "Very well.
The official then took leave of the people and sent them back; they immediately felt as if they were falling from a great height, then suddenly revived and regained their lives.
The parents then placed him in a carriage and went to the Jetavana to inform the Buddha.

The Buddha called out to the man and questioned him; he answered with what he had seen and what he had said. The Buddha then smiled, and five-colored light issued from the crown of his head, circled his body three times, and returned to enter through his navel.
Ānanda then adjusted his robes, knelt with one knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha does not smile without cause; there must be a specific meaning for this smile. I pray that the Buddha will explain its significance in detail!"
The Buddha said:
"Ānanda! Listen attentively and receive this, along with the assembled multitude."
Ānanda received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:

"In this world of Jambudvīpa, it is an age of the five heinous crimes; sons are unfilial toward their fathers, ministers are disloyal toward their sovereigns, and husbands and wives deceive one another, while those above deceive those below."
The people are stubborn and perverse, possessing little sense of righteousness or principle; they are arrogant and lack self-restraint, using the strong to oppress the weak.
The wealthy associate with the wealthy, while the poor remain in their destitution; they are greedy for profit and stingy, devoid of compassion, seeking only to surpass others.
The Four Heavenly Kings guard [the gates], while malevolent spirits and deities watch for their opportunity.

Those who violate [the precepts] shall die; their souls and spirits will wander through successive rebirths, receiving retribution according to their deeds: they shall become hungry ghosts or animals, or suffer the agonizing torments of hell—being lashed, flogged, and hacked, or boiled and roasted in cauldrons of boiling water.

If there remains even a slight merit, one may attain rebirth in the heavens; specifically, one will dwell in the sixth heaven, the Heaven of Māra. There, with meager merit and short lifespan, one will not receive the teachings of the Dharma.
Even if one attains birth as a human, one will become a lowly slave or servant;

or one may become a beast such as an ox, horse, mule, donkey, camel, elephant, tiger, lion, bird, animal, insect, or moth. Such suffering is beyond description, and for hundreds, thousands, or tens of thousands of kalpas, one will find no liberation.
At birth they are immediately afflicted by disease, or they die at once.
Even if they obtain human form, their six sense faculties are incomplete; they are humpbacked, crippled, deaf, blind, mute, or paralyzed—suffering such boundless misery.

"Now, there is one person in this world who knows that there is a Buddha in the world, hears the Dharma of the sutras, and meets the community of bhikṣus; possessing a virtuous mind, a benevolent intention, reverence, and compassion, they abandon the ninety-six kinds of heterodox paths to enter the True Dharma. They reflect upon themselves and discipline themselves to receive and uphold the five precepts, practicing the ten wholesome deeds to extinguish the ten unwholesome deeds."

At that time, there was a person who had all attained the Way during the era of Vipaśyin Buddha; his merit was equal to that of this person, and whatever offenses he had committed over hundreds, thousands, or tens of thousands of kalpas were all completely extinguished.
After that person’s life has ended, they shall never again behold the three evil realms.

Even if they have committed transgressions, when they are summoned to the hells according to the gravity of their offenses, the King of Hell will see them and his hair shall stand on end; he will look up to that person with reverence, and neither the sovereign nor the common people will fail to honor and revere them. Although they have not yet attained the Way, their merit is so magnificent and brilliant that gods, humans, dragons, and ghosts all praise them.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

“After my parinirvāṇa, many people in the world will fail to revere the Dharma; they will delight in self-exaltation and arrogance, looking down upon others, treating the True Dharma with contempt, and slandering the bhikṣus. They will not provide them with alms, and they will revile them, striking them with tiles and stones, without any sense of restraint or fear.”
People of this sort have all come from the realm of Māra; because they have been born as humans, they are again thus evil.

Those who believe in and delight in the Buddha-dharma were, in fact, the foremost disciples of the Buddhas in ancient and former ages. They were able to discern the true from the false and followed the True Dharma accordingly; they upheld the sutras and precepts and further extinguished twenty matters. All such individuals are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they are certainly not ordinary people!
"In human life there must be death; there is no one who does not die.

A person of virtue who upholds the precepts does not begrudge their own body or life, but contemplates only great kindness and great compassion to rescue and deliver all beings, acting as a guide and leader for the multitude."
The Bodhisattva does not fear the transformations of birth and death; he enters into birth and death to deliver beings from birth and death.
He enters the hells to preach the sutras and precepts, restraining evil and promoting good;
he enters the realm of hungry ghosts to preach on the practice of giving.
Entering among animals, he preaches to them that licentiousness causes one to lose their human body;
being born among the heavens, he teaches the various devas;
and among humans, he establishes the practice of transforming evil into good.
When a person performs the deeds of hell, they have the perception of hell;
when a person performs the deeds of animals, they have the perception of animals;
when a person performs the deeds of devas, they have the perception of devas.
When a person performs the deeds of a hungry ghost, they have the perception of a hungry ghost;
when a person performs the deeds of a human, they have the perception of a human.
All phenomena are ultimately non-existent; it is only by relying on what is performed that names arise and conceptual thoughts follow.

Now, this worthy one has clearly witnessed the evidence with his own eyes; having been born into this world as a human, possessing merit and virtue and upholding the True Dharma, why not exert yourself so that you may personally attain the noble status of a Buddha?
"Why do you perform such laborious deeds?
You yourself must go and undergo their results; what benefit is there in regret?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"When the Dharma is about to flourish, good people are born into the world;
when the Dharma is about to decline, evil people become numerous.
Let us inform one another and each diligently apply ourselves with vigor to the sutras and precepts, taking heed of the impermanence of all things."
The power of impermanence is great; the Buddha does not abide eternally.
Strive with diligence in this world, and having already delivered yourself, you will further be able to rescue and deliver all humans and non-humans.
"O Bhikṣus! While I am still in this world, you must exert yourselves; do not say that the Buddha will always remain. If you do not strive now, what benefit will it be to regret it later?"
"Now, those who were called 'the dead' are known as those who have realized the Truth (dṛṣṭasatya).

Upon hearing the Buddha preach this sutra, the parents and all members of their families attained the Noble Truth of Arhatship; they immediately attained the stage of Avaivartika (non-retrogression), remaining firm and no longer wavering.

The bhikṣus, the bodhisattvas, the great disciples, the devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits, having heard this sutra, were all filled with joy; they all came forward to pay homage to the Buddha and then departed.
The Scripture on the Disciple’s Death and Rebirth
